candidates.name: Art Is Never Finished, Only Abandoned
candidates.aphorism_text: A work of art is never finished, it is abandoned.
candidates.attribution: Attributed to Leonardo da Vinci / Paul Valery; Bannard aphorism #25
candidates.description: Reframes completion as a decision, not a state. Transfers powerfully to software (shipping vs. polishing), writing (deadlines vs. perfection), and any craft where 'done' is a judgment call, not an objective fact. Encodes the tension between aspiration and pragmatism.

candidates.name: Constraint Enables Creativity
candidates.aphorism_text: Convention and restriction release inhibition and provoke the imagination.
candidates.attribution: Walter Darby Bannard, Aphorisms for Artists
candidates.description: The counterintuitive principle that limitation increases creative output. Bannard's formulation is precise: restriction doesn't merely permit creativity, it actively 'provokes' it. Transfers to software architecture (API constraints), writing (sonnets, haiku), game design (limited mechanics), and organizational design (bounded autonomy).

candidates.name: Too Much Freedom Inhibits Choice
candidates.aphorism_text: Too much freedom inhibits choice. Constructive narrowness clarifies choice.
candidates.attribution: Walter Darby Bannard, Aphorisms for Artists
candidates.description: The paradox of choice expressed as studio wisdom. Maps directly onto UX design (feature bloat), product management (scope), and personal productivity (decision fatigue). Bannard's 'constructive narrowness' is a design principle disguised as art advice.

candidates.name: See First, Name Later
candidates.attribution: Walter Darby Bannard, Aphorisms for Artists
candidates.description: Prioritizing perception over categorization. Naming something forces it into existing mental categories, potentially losing what makes it novel. Transfers to user research (observe before theorizing), debugging (read the error before guessing), scientific method (data before hypothesis), and any domain where premature labeling blocks genuine understanding.

candidates.name: Grabbing Attention vs. Rewarding Attention
candidates.aphorism_text: There's a big difference between grabbing attention and rewarding attention.
candidates.attribution: Walter Darby Bannard, Aphorisms for Artists
candidates.description: Distinguishes spectacle from substance. The attention economy makes this more relevant than ever: clickbait grabs attention; good journalism rewards it. Flashy UI grabs attention; well-designed UX rewards it. Applies to marketing, content creation, architecture, product design, and teaching.

candidates.name: Without the Eye the Head Is Blind
candidates.aphorism_text: Without the eye, the head is blind. Without the head, the eye is adrift.
candidates.attribution: Walter Darby Bannard, Aphorisms for Artists
candidates.description: Perception and analysis are complementary, not competing. Neither intuition alone nor intellect alone suffices. Transfers to data science (data without theory vs. theory without data), management (metrics without context vs. context without metrics), and design (aesthetics without usability vs. usability without aesthetics). An opposed-pair encoding a permanent professional tension.

candidates.name: Form Follows Function
candidates.aphorism_text: Form ever follows function, and this is the law.
candidates.attribution: Louis Sullivan, 'The Tall Office Building Artistically Considered' (1896)
candidates.description: The dominant design principle of the 20th century. Sullivan's architectural dictum became the organizing metaphor for industrial design, software architecture, UX, and organizational structure. The source frame (biology: eagle's wing shape follows flight function) maps structure onto any domain where appearance should derive from purpose. Spawned the counter-aphorism 'less is a bore' (Venturi).

candidates.name: Less Is More
candidates.attribution: Robert Browning (1855); adopted by Mies van der Rohe; countered by Robert Venturi ('Less is a bore', 1966)
candidates.description: Minimalism as a design philosophy. The aphorism encodes a deep structural claim: removing elements can increase value, not just reduce cost. Transfers to writing (concision), software (feature discipline), communication (brevity), cooking (few ingredients, high quality), and music (negative space). One half of the most famous opposed pair in design history.

candidates.name: Negative Space Is as Important as Positive Space
candidates.aphorism_text: Negative space is as important as positive space.
candidates.description: What you leave out defines what you put in. The visual arts principle that the space around and between subjects is not empty but actively shapes perception. Transfers to music (silence between notes), writing (what is left unsaid), UI design (whitespace), architecture (void vs. solid), and rhetoric (the power of omission). The issue specifically calls this out as a canonical cross-domain metaphor.

candidates.name: Kill Your Darlings
candidates.attribution: Arthur Quiller-Couch, On the Art of Writing (1916); related to Bannard's 'Keep your ego out of your art'
candidates.description: Delete the parts you love most if they don't serve the whole. Originally about overwritten prose, now applies to product management (cutting favorite features), software engineering (removing clever code), filmmaking (cutting favorite scenes), and any creative endeavor where attachment to one's best work can damage the overall product.

candidates.name: Art Is Making Something Better Without Knowing What Better Is
candidates.aphorism_text: Art is making something better without knowing what better is until you make it.
candidates.attribution: Walter Darby Bannard, Aphorisms for Artists
candidates.description: Quality as emergent, not predetermined. You cannot specify what 'good' looks like in advance; you recognize it only through the act of making. Transfers to iterative design (prototyping to discover requirements), agile software development (working software reveals what's needed), startup methodology (build to learn), and research (the question clarifies only through investigation).

candidates.name: Intuition Precedes Analysis
candidates.aphorism_text: Always let intuitive perception precede analysis.
candidates.attribution: Walter Darby Bannard, Aphorisms for Artists
candidates.description: The visual arts principle that you should experience before you explain. Connects to Kahneman's System 1/System 2 framework. Transfers to user testing (watch users before analyzing metrics), wine tasting (taste before reading the label), code review (read for feel before checking style rules), and any evaluative process where premature analysis corrupts the signal.

candidates.name: Remedy Mistakes by Taking Advantage of Them
candidates.aphorism_text: In art as in life, the best way to remedy mistakes is to take advantage of them.
candidates.attribution: Walter Darby Bannard, Aphorisms for Artists
candidates.description: Errors as generative material, not defects to undo. The painter who turns a drip into a design element. Transfers to jazz (wrong notes become new chord), entrepreneurship (pivot), scientific research (serendipitous discovery), and software (bugs revealing unintended but useful behaviors). Reframes failure from loss to opportunity.

candidates.name: Good Art Carries a High Density of Choice
candidates.aphorism_text: Good art, no matter how simple or casual-seeming, always carries a high density of choice.
candidates.attribution: Walter Darby Bannard, Aphorisms for Artists
candidates.description: Quality correlates with decisions per unit, not effort per unit. Something that looks effortless may encode hundreds of deliberate choices. Transfers to writing (every word in a poem is chosen), cooking (simple dishes with precise technique), code (elegant solutions that embody many rejected alternatives), and design (minimalist interfaces reflecting extensive iteration).

candidates.name: The Work Replaces Your Ideas with Its Ideas
candidates.aphorism_text: Start a painting with fresh ideas, and then let the painting replace your ideas with its ideas.
candidates.attribution: Walter Darby Bannard, Aphorisms for Artists
candidates.description: The work-in-progress has agency. What you intended is less important than what the material wants to become. Transfers to writing (characters 'taking over' the story), software architecture (the codebase developing its own grain), organizational design (culture emerging from structure), and research (the data redirecting the hypothesis). Personifies the artifact as a collaborator.

candidates.name: Art Is a Battle, a Mill That Grinds
candidates.aphorism_text: Art is not a pleasure trip. It is a battle, a mill that grinds.
candidates.attribution: Jean-Francois Millet, in Binyon, The Mind of the Artist
candidates.description: Creative work as combat and industrial labor. Romanticized notions of inspired effortlessness are replaced by metaphors of grinding, struggle, and endurance. Transfers to software engineering (the grind of debugging), writing (the war of attrition against the blank page), and any sustained creative effort where persistence matters more than inspiration.

candidates.name: Work Should Look Easy, However Elaborate
candidates.aphorism_text: Work should always look as though it had been done with ease, however elaborate.
candidates.attribution: John Everett Millais, in Binyon, The Mind of the Artist
candidates.description: Sprezzatura in the visual arts: the craft of concealing craft. The effort should be invisible in the result. Transfers to public speaking (rehearsed spontaneity), UI design (simple interfaces hiding complex systems), writing (prose that reads effortlessly), and performance (athletes making it look easy). Related to Castiglione's Renaissance ideal.
